bib.title: A Survey of Resource-Efficient LLM and Multimodal Foundation Models

read.skipped: Reference list (refs [46]-[497], about 63k chars) skimmed only (first 45 entries and the tail read); no appendix exists. Everything from the title to the conclusions (lines 1-3140 of the cached text) was read line by line.

question: How do current algorithm and system techniques make large language, vision, diffusion and multimodal foundation models cheaper in compute, memory, storage and energy across training and serving?
contributions: A cost analysis of language, vision and multimodal foundation models (Section 2).

A taxonomy of resource-efficient architectures (Section 3), algorithms for pre-training, fine-tuning, inference and compression (Section 4), and systems for distributed training, federated learning, cloud serving and edge serving (Section 5).
Six future directions (Section 6): cloud-edge hybrid deployment, model sparsity, LLM as a service, agents as a system to optimize, privacy-preserving FMs, and the scaling law.

results.claim: KV cache memory in single precision is B x S x D x L x 2 x 4 bytes (batch, sequence length, hidden size, decoder layers, K and V, FP32 bytes).
results.setup: Formula for a Transformer decoder; the 4 is the byte size of an FP32 value (use 2 for FP16, which the survey does not state).
results.quote: the memory required for storing the KV cache in single-precision format can be calculated as (B × S × D × L × 2 × 4) Bytes
results.note: No model, hardware or worked number is given; the formula assumes full multi-head K and V (no GQA or MQA), which the survey does not say.

results.claim: Attention compute is quadratic and FFN compute linear in sequence length, and a KV cache cuts the recomputation at the cost of extra memory.
results.source: Li et al. [244], cited for the complexity statement
results.setup: T is sequence length, D hidden size; the GPT-2 FLOPs curve (Fig. 5) was produced with the flops-profiler tool.
results.quote: the computation complexity of attention is O(T 2D), while that of FFN is O(TD2), where T represents the sequence length and D the hidden state dimension of the model [244]

results.claim: Most sparse-attention designs cut compute but do not necessarily shrink KV cache memory, because shrinking the cache needs tokens that are dropped never to be read again.
results.setup: Conceptual point in Section 4.3.3, citing Longformer [36] and BigBird [464] as the compute-oriented designs.
results.quote: most sparse attention designs, which primarily target the reduction of computational complexity [36, 464], do not necessarily lead to a reduction in KV cache memory consumption.

results.claim: H2O, which evicts KV tokens by attention score, is quoted as cutting latency up to 1.9x and raising throughput 29x.
results.setup: Against unnamed 'robust baselines'; model, hardware, batch size and cache budget are not stated by the survey.
results.quote: H2O demonstrates the capability to reduce latency by up to 1.9× and increase throughput by 29×.

results.claim: Scissorhands is quoted as reducing KV cache inference memory up to 5x while maintaining model quality.
results.setup: Compact-KV-cache inference; model, task and baseline not stated by the survey.
results.quote: achieving up to a 5× reduction while maintaining model quality

results.claim: Dynamic Context Pruning, which learns KV eviction during pre-training, is quoted as giving up to 2x inference throughput.
results.setup: Eviction strategy learned at pre-training time; baseline and hardware not stated.
results.quote: This approach has demonstrated the ability to achieve up to a 2× increase in inference throughput and even greater memory savings.

results.claim: vAttention, which lets the OS/CUDA remap physical memory instead of a custom paged kernel, is quoted as up to 1.29x the throughput of vLLM.
results.setup: End-to-end serving; the survey gives no model, hardware or workload.
results.quote: It further improves the end-to-end serving throughput by up to 1.29× compared to vLLM.

results.claim: vLLM manages the KV cache as OS-style blocks and its block-based attention gives results identical to standard attention.
results.setup: Section 4.3.3; no memory-saving figure is given for vLLM in this survey.
results.quote: The computation results of this block-based attention mechanism are identical to those of the standard attention mechanism.

results.claim: The cloud serving section describes the two-phase generation process: prefill processes all input tokens and fills the KV cache, decoding processes only the new token and updates it.
results.source: LightSeq [398] credited with proposing the KV cache
results.setup: Section 5.3, for LLM serving.
results.quote: The prefill phase processes all input tokens of a request and stores the intermediate states in KV cache.
results.note: Crediting LightSeq with 'proposing' the KV cache conflicts with the earlier mention in Section 2.1.1 that the KV cache is from [76], which is a reference the survey uses for FlashAttention.

results.claim: Splitwise splits prefill and decoding onto different machines, SARATHI and DeepSpeed-FastGen chunk the prefill and schedule it with decode.
results.setup: Qualitative, no numbers; Section 5.3.1.
results.quote: Splitwise [308] splits the prefill phase and the decoding phase onto different machines according to their different computation and memory requirements.

results.claim: Orca batches at iteration granularity so finished requests return early and new requests start after one iteration.
results.setup: Qualitative, no numbers; Section 5.3.1.
results.quote: Orca [458] proposes selective batching and iteration-level scheduling to batch requests of different lengths at the granularity of iterations to increase the maximum batch size.

results.claim: Prompt Cache, which precomputes attention states for frequent prompt segments, is quoted as 8x faster on GPU and 60x on CPU with output accuracy preserved.
results.setup: Reuse of cached attention states of frequent text segments; the survey states neither the metric nor the models.
results.quote: The enhancements vary from an 8× improvement for GPU-based inference to a 60× improvement for CPU-based inference, all while preserving output accuracy

results.claim: Speculative decoding is lossless; the survey quotes 2-3x on T5X, a similar speedup on a 70B Chinchilla, 2.13x for SpecTr and 1.73x for Draft & Verify on Llama-2.
results.source: Leviathan et al. [209]; Chen et al. [54]; SpecTr [368]; Draft & Verify [470]
results.setup: A small model Mq drafts tokens and the large model Mp verifies them in one forward pass.
results.quote: Yaniv et al. [209] achieves 2-3× improvement using speculative decoding on the T5X model.
results.note: The survey's description says 'decode γ tokens by Mp', which should be the draft model Mq.

results.claim: ATOM with 4-bit weight-activation quantization is quoted as up to 7.73x the serving throughput of FP16 and 2.53x that of INT8 at the same latency target.
results.setup: Serving at the same latency target; model and hardware not stated by the survey.
results.quote: ATOM on 4-bit weight-activation quantization improves end-to-end throughput by up to 7.73× compared to the FP16 and by 2.53× compared to INT8 quantization, while maintaining the same latency target.

results.claim: LLM-FP4 quantizes LLaMA-13B weights and activations to 4-bit floating point with 8.4% accuracy loss.
results.setup: LLaMA-13B, 4-bit weights and activations; the survey names no benchmark and does not say whether the loss is relative or in points.
results.quote: LLM-FP4 successfully quantizes both weights and activations in the LLaMA-13B to only 4-bit and achieves only 8.4% accuracy loss than the full-precision model.

results.claim: llama.cpp K-quant inference is quoted as about 3-4x faster than the original FP16 model.
results.setup: K-quant on llama.cpp; hardware and model not stated.
results.quote: llama.cpp demonstrates that performing model inference using K-quant quantization is approximately 3-4 × faster than inference with the original FP16 model.

results.claim: PowerInfer, splitting hot neurons to the GPU and cold neurons to the CPU, is quoted as up to 11x faster than llama.cpp, running a 40B model at ten tokens per second on a PC.
results.setup: Personal computer with a GPU plus CPU; the survey does not name the hardware.
results.quote: PowerInfer achieves up to 11× acceleration, enabling the 40B model to output ten tokens per second on a personal computer.

results.claim: LLMLingua is quoted as compressing prompts up to 20x with minimal performance loss.
results.setup: Prompt compression before the model call; tasks and models not stated.
results.quote: LLMLingua can achieve up to 20× compression with minimal performance loss.

results.claim: Pre-training LLaMA-2-70B is quoted at 1.7 million GPU hours, 2.5x10^12 J and 291 tons CO2e.
results.setup: Pre-training of LLaMA-2-70B; the survey does not repeat the hardware.
results.quote: the pre-training of LLaMa-2-70B takes 1.7× millions of GPU hours and consumes 2.5 × 1012 Joules of energy.
results.note: Section 4.1 says 'LLaMa-70B [383] takes 1.7 × 106 GPU hours' and Section 4.1.1 says '0.3 trillion tokens for GPT-3-175B', which is the survey's own figure.

results.claim: NVIDIA would need to ship 1.5 million AI servers a year by 2027, using at least 85.4 TWh a year.
results.setup: Projection, servers at full capacity, from the survey's Fig. 1 source [81].
results.quote: These servers, running at full capacity, would consume at least 85.4 terawatt-hours of electricity annuall
results.note: The PDF text is truncated at 'annuall'.

results.claim: A Vicuna-7B LLM module in a multimodal model has 7B parameters, 14 GB memory and 312 GFLOPs per sample, far above the encoders.
results.setup: Fig. 6(b), PandaGPT-style integrated Vicuna-7B; the input length is not stated. This is the survey's own profiling, with no method detail.
results.quote: this model consists of 7B parameters, occupies 14G memory, and with total GFLOPs of 312 for processing a sample

results.claim: Stable Diffusion 2.1 U-Net has 865M parameters and 759G FLOPs per sample.
results.setup: Latents 4x96x96, a 10-token prompt, from Fig. 7; one denoising pass is implied but not stated.
results.quote: The U-Net has 865M parameters, with total FLOPs of 759G for processing a sample.

results.claim: Mamba is quoted as 5x faster than Transformers with linear scaling in sequence length, and RetNet as 25-50% less training memory and 7x faster training.
results.setup: Baselines, hardware and sizes not stated by the survey.
results.quote: This model achieves a notable 5× speed increase over traditional transformers and exhibits linear scaling with sequence length.

results.claim: Table 4 lists time and space complexity: the Transformer is O(T^2 d) time, O(T^2 + Td) space; RWKV is O(Td) time, O(d) space.
results.source: Vaswani et al. [388] and the variants' own papers
results.setup: T is sequence length, d hidden size.
results.table: Table 4, rows Transformer and RWKV, columns Time and Space

limits: Authors state the scope is algorithms and systems only; hardware design is excluded, and 'resource' means physical resources, not training data or privacy (Section 1).
Authors state they survey mainly CSRankings top-venue papers plus hand-picked arXiv papers, mainly after 2020 (Section 1).

It runs no experiments of its own beyond the FLOPs and parameter profiling in Section 2; every speedup in Sections 3 to 5 is the cited paper's claim, usually with the model, hardware, batch size and baseline missing, so figures from different papers cannot be compared.
The cloud serving section (5.3) is under two pages, qualitative and without numbers; the edge section has none.

Coverage ends around mid-2024 (v2 is dated 23 Sep 2024; the latest items are QuaRot, EfficientQAT, I-LLM, SpinQuant, DeepSeek-V2, Mooncake); no FP8 or MXFP4 serving, no EAGLE-style speculative decoding, no reasoning-model serving.
Speculative decoding is described with a notation slip (draft tokens decoded 'by Mp'), and the PowerInfer/SIGE passage reuses reference [352] for two different works.
practices: Use a KV cache to avoid recomputing keys and values, and budget its memory as B x S x D x L x 2 x bytes per value (Section 2.1.3).
Treat KV memory and attention compute as separate problems: sparse attention alone does not shrink the cache unless dropped tokens are never read again (Section 4.3.3).
Manage the KV cache in blocks allocated on demand rather than contiguously, as vLLM's PagedAttention does (Sections 4.3.3 and 5.3.2).
Use iteration-level scheduling and selective batching so short requests leave early and new ones join each iteration (Section 5.3.1, Orca).
Chunk the prefill and interleave it with decoding, or place prefill and decode on different machines, to limit prefill interference (Section 5.3.1, SARATHI, DeepSpeed-FastGen, Splitwise).
Use a prefill-oriented kernel (FlashAttention) for prefill and a decode-specific kernel (Flash-Decoding, FlashDecoding++) for decoding (Section 5.3.1).
Offload parameters and activations to DRAM or NVMe when GPU memory is short (Section 5.3.2).
Reuse precomputed attention states for frequent prompt segments to cut latency (Section 4.3.1, Prompt Cache).

terms.definition: Stores intermediate states of the attention mechanism at each step, which prevents recalculation of tokens processed in earlier steps, at an additional storage or memory cost.
Processes all input tokens of a request and stores the intermediate states in the KV cache.
Only needs to process the computation related to the newly generated tokens and update the KV cache accordingly.
Autoregressive generation of sequences with a cost-efficient small model, followed by parallel verification of each token by a larger model.
vLLM adopts the concept of paged memory in operating systems and manages the KV cache, which is susceptible to memory fragmentation, as blocks.
